ActionResultResourceKind.description:
What a write tool created or changed, as the console's resource vocabulary.

The set is exactly the non-READ_ONLY tools whose result carries an
identifier something can be opened by. A tool that writes nothing
addressable reports no resource rather than a kind nobody can route to:
``request_human_handoff`` opens a SupportCase whose id the escalation never
returns, ``set_profile_name`` and ``record_engagement_intent`` change the
invoking user's own account, and ``propose_form_values`` writes nothing.

ActionRisk.description:
Risk classification of a tool action (platform ADR 0089 / 0096 / 0097).

READ_ONLY actions run without asking. Every public write is approved as part
of an action plan (platform ADR 0196): a BENIGN_WRITE step may be covered by the
user's auto-approval for that operation, a DESTRUCTIVE one never is.

For a public operation the tier is derived from the route (method, custom
verb, declared overrides) and authorization is the route's own gate. For a
native tool, BENIGN_WRITE is a safe change the invoking user is always
entitled to — requesting a human handoff must never be refused (platform ADR 0097).
ActionRisk.title: ActionRisk

ActionVisibility.description:
Whether a person is shown an action, or it is an attempt the assistant corrected itself.

``INTERNAL`` marks a refused or failed attempt the model reads and recovers
from on its own — a read that failed, a plan refused before anyone saw it, a
repeat the guard turned away. It stays on the record; clients may fold it
away. When the run itself fails, its INTERNAL actions become ``USER`` again,
because nothing recovered from them.
ActionVisibility.title: ActionVisibility

AssignedTaskStopReason.description:
Why an ended task's work stopped.

COMPLETED: the assistant finished. STEP_CEILING: it used its steps.
BUDGET_EXHAUSTED: it spent its budget. TRUNCATED: its last reply was cut off.
FAILED: it failed. CANCELLED: you cancelled the task. EXPIRED: the deadline
passed. SUPERSEDED: the work was replaced. NOT_STARTED: the assistant could
not start the work (its thread was busy, or the organization reached its
assistant spend cap); the task FAILED.

AssistantUpdateKind.description:
What an assistant update tells the person while a run works (Pelorus ADR 0009).

An update is an ASSISTANT turn that is not the reply: it survives a reload and
shows in every tab, but it is never replayed into a later prompt, and a run's
updates count once toward unread with its reply. ``ACKNOWLEDGEMENT`` is what
the assistant understood and will do next, posted before the work;
``STILL_WORKING`` says a run that has shown nothing for a while is still at
it; ``MILESTONE`` is a server-written line for something the platform
observed (a plan approved, a step done, a check settled).

CreateBlueprintRequest.description:
Body for ``POST /v1/organizations/{organization_id}/blueprints``.

``document`` is any JSON object, judged by the apply pipeline rather than
refused by the request — the one document body on this surface that is.
Creation is where the blueprint is *named*, and a caller who names it
nowhere is given a minted slug, which the platform writes into the
document before it validates it. A typed body could not express that: the
released bundle requires ``metadata.slug``, so the typed view mirrors it
and would 422 the slug-less document at the boundary, before anything
could mint one. The bundle still judges it a moment later, in the
structural phase, and the same diagnostics come back.

document.description: The blueprint v2 document of the first version, as JSON. Its metadata.revision is the revision the draft is created at; its components are named by published UUID and revision. Its metadata.slug may be omitted, and is then the slug above or a minted one.
document.title: Document

slug.description: DNS-label name of the blueprint, new to the organization's library. Defaults to the document's metadata.slug, which must equal it; a friendly name is minted when neither is given.
slug.title: Slug

FormFieldWriteTier.description:
How the console may apply a value the assistant proposes for a field.

``AUTO`` — applied live, marked, and undoable in one click.
``CONFIRM`` — rendered as a proposal card; nothing moves until the user clicks.
``WITHHELD`` — never proposed. A secret (``isSensitive``) or a
platform-generated (``generator``) parameter. A WITHHELD field is described to
the model only as a *count* — never by key or label — so a prompt-injection
attempt has no field name to attach itself to, and its value is dropped at
ingest so it never reaches the append-only context snapshot.

The tier is decided by the **client**, from its own live form, and re-derived
there at apply time; the server echoes it as a rendering hint and additionally
refuses WITHHELD proposals. It is never an authorization on its own.

its own live form — writing the safe ones, offering the rest as a card — and it
never submits the form. Echoing ``writeTier`` lets the server refuse a WITHHELD
proposal before the wire, and makes the persisted block self-describing for
Backstage replay, which has no access to the console's form registry.

MessageDeliveryMode.description:
What a user message does to an assistant run still working on the thread.

``QUEUE`` waits: the message starts the next run once the live one ends,
so typing never cancels work in flight or answers a pending approval.
``INTERRUPT`` is the explicit "Interrupt & send": the live run is cancelled
and the message starts a run now. With nothing live the two are the same.

attachBlockReason.description: Precondition the attach loop is waiting on before it can mount the volume, or null when nothing is blocking it. AWAITING_PLACEMENT means no host has been chosen for the workload yet — the ordinary opening state of every volume. AWAITING_HOST_OVERLAY means the chosen host has no private-network address yet. AWAITING_ZONE means the workload runs in another zone of the region than the one holding the volume, or in another region, from where the volume may not be attached; it attaches once the workload is placed in the volume's zone. None is a failure: the volume waits without consuming retry attempts and attaches automatically once the precondition clears.

AWAITING_PLACEMENT means the component the volume belongs to has not been placed yet; the volume is created where that component runs, and provisions automatically once it is placed. INSUFFICIENT_STORAGE_NODES means fewer storage nodes are online than the volume's durability tier requires, and the volume provisions automatically once capacity returns. STORAGE_FLEET_UNAVAILABLE means enough storage nodes exist but the storage service is not currently accepting new volumes; the platform is restoring it and the volume provisions automatically once it is back. All three are deliberately exempt from the provisioning deadline and are never failed for waiting.

PlatformRegionStatus.description:
Catalog lifecycle of a vendor-neutral PlatformRegion (Pelorus ADR 0122 §6).

A region the code seeds takes the status its registry gives it, and only a
code release changes that. A region an admin opens starts in ``PREVIEW`` and
turns ``ACTIVE`` once its first zone comes online; nothing else moves it
(SiteRegister.PlatformRegion#4). Bring-online itself lives on the ``Zone``
that binds to the region.

``PREVIEW`` is offered to no customer: every customer read leaves a region
in preview out, while the operator's reads list it with its status.
``DEPRECATED`` is sunsetting: customers still see it, and it takes no new
zone. No ``UNSPECIFIED`` sentinel (AIP-126 / schema-design).
PlatformRegionStatus.title: PlatformRegionStatus

PromptCacheRetention.description:
Whether an alias asks the vendor to cache the request's prompt, and for how long.

An endpoint owner's choice, never the caller's: a cache write costs more
than an uncached token and a cache read far less, so turning it on changes
what every call through the alias costs. Only some vendors take a
per-request cache instruction; others cache long prompts on their own. An
alias may ask for a cache only when every vendor that can serve it takes
the instruction, and a write that asks otherwise is refused (422).

RunTriggerKind.description:
Why a run exists — never its Status, which is the FSM's word.

``USER_MESSAGE`` — a posted USER turn started it, and ``trigger_message_id``
names that turn.
``GREETING`` — the console opened the assistant against a form and the user
typed nothing. A GREETING run has **no trigger message**, because nothing was
appended to the transcript: the user never reads a turn they did not write,
and the opening directive rides the run's own operation instead.
``CONTINUATION`` — the user chose Continue on a run that stopped at its step
ceiling (STEP_CEILING) or whose reply was cut off (TRUNCATED).
``RETRY`` — the user chose Retry on a run that FAILED.

A CONTINUATION or RETRY run is a **successor**: ``continues_run_id`` names the
ended run it carries on from, and, like a greeting, it writes no message — its
directive rides the run's operation (platform ADR 0206). It answers the same user turn
as its predecessor, so it inherits that run's ``trigger_message_id``.
``AGENDA`` — a follow-up or a watch the assistant scheduled fired. Like a
greeting it has no trigger message.
RunTriggerKind.title: RunTriggerKind

post.description:
Start a run that continues one which stopped at its step budget or was cut off.

The run must have ended COMPLETED with stop reason STEP_CEILING or TRUNCATED,
be the newest run on its thread, and belong to a conversation that is open to
the assistant. The new run has trigger kind CONTINUATION and names the ended
run in `continuesRunId`. No message is posted: the thread shows only what the
user wrote, and the new run's replies. Returns 202 with the new run, which is
queued and reports its progress like any other run, and a `Location` header
naming it. Send an `Idempotency-Key` to make a retried request replay that
response; without one, a second call starts nothing and answers 409
`NOT_LATEST`, naming the new run in `latestRunId`.

parameters.description: Opaque client-chosen key that makes this call safe to retry (IETF httpapi draft). Send the same key with the same request body and a successful response is replayed verbatim, carrying `Idempotent-Replayed: true`. A rejected or failed request releases the key, so a corrected resubmit runs for real. Keys are remembered for 24 hours.
parameters.name: Idempotency-Key

404.description: The run does not exist, or its thread is not the caller's

409.description: Nothing was started (`/errors/resource-conflict`). The `reason` extension member says why: `NOT_CONTINUABLE` (the run's ending does not allow it), `NOT_LATEST` (a later run already started on its thread), `THREAD_BUSY` (a run is live on that thread) or `CONVERSATION_NOT_OPEN` (a person is handling the conversation). `latestRunId` names the run to look at instead (the newest run, or the live one), or is null

429.description: Nothing was started (`/errors/assistant-spend-limit-reached`): the organization has reached the assistant's spending limit for the current window. It clears on its own; adding credit does not lift it

default.description: An RFC 9457 problem document. Returned for any error status this operation does not document explicitly.

post.summary: Continue a run that stopped early

post.description:
Start a run that tries a failed run's last step again.

The run must have ended FAILED, be the newest run on its thread, and belong to
a conversation that is open to the assistant. The new run has trigger kind
RETRY and names the failed run in `continuesRunId`. No message is posted.
Returns 202 with the new run, which is queued and reports its progress like
any other run, and a `Location` header naming it. Send an `Idempotency-Key` to
make a retried request replay that response; without one, a second call

want in words, and the slug lookup when they name a specific app.

Estimate what running a listing's blueprint costs per hour and per month.

Prices one replica of every node at today's compute rates, the ones the
deploy form shows, and sums them. Only compute is included; storage,

costs nothing. ``complete`` is false when a node's compute profile has no
price, and ``rateStatus`` is PLACEHOLDER while any rate summed is a launch
figure. Answers 404 for a listing the detail read does not resolve, and 409
for a COMPONENT listing, which deploys nothing.

get.description:
The posted credit balance at the end of each UTC day, from `from` to `to` inclusive, at most 90 days. `to` defaults to today (UTC) and may not be later; `from` defaults to the 30 days ending at `to`.

These are the ledger's balances, not past values of Available Spend. Pending Charges are not on the ledger until they are posted, so no point includes them. A point is the credit held less what the organization owes, so it is below zero when the organization owes more than it holds. An expired grant leaves only once its expiry is posted, after it lapses, and an amount owed or a reversal from before `owedMinor` existed stays on the ledger alone. A point, today's included, can therefore differ from the Prepaid Balance plus Promotional Credits less the `owedMinor` that `GET .../balance` reports.

post.description:
Create a new blueprint from scratch in an organization, holding its first draft.

A blueprint is an app: the components it runs, how they connect, and the
compute and exposure each gets. The smallest draft is a document of
``specVersion: v2``, ``kind: BLUEPRINT``, ``metadata`` with ``revision: 1``
and ``spec`` with an empty ``components`` map; components are then added
one at a time with ``attach_blueprint_version_component``, and each node
is given compute (``set_blueprint_version_compute``), parameters and
bindings for its inputs, and any PUBLIC endpoint. To copy an app from the
catalog instead, use ``clone_blueprint_from_listing``.

The draft is created at the document's ``metadata.revision``. The ``slug``
must be new to the organization's library; an existing blueprint takes a
new version instead (``POST /v1/blueprints/{blueprint_id}/versions``).
Name the blueprint nowhere — no ``slug``, no ``metadata.slug`` — and a
friendly ``adjective-noun`` name is minted and written into the stored
document. A blueprint written through the API names its components by
published UUID and revision. A document the schema accepts is stored even
when a semantic rule fails: the returned ``validation`` names what keeps
it from publishing.

Requires the ``blueprints:create`` permission.

Returns VALID, INVALID or INCOMPLETE with every diagnostic, stopping at
the first phase that fails. STRUCTURAL runs the parser and the schema.

document names as the organization sees them. PUBLICATION adds the
admission rules a publish decides from the document (a description, at
least one node) and reports platform admission deferred, so its best
answer is INCOMPLETE; DEPLOYMENT also defers deployment resolution.

would refuse in the document and its components is previewed as WARNING
diagnostics only: they never change the status, and a deploy still runs
admission itself. With ``within``, the document is validated in that
stored blueprint version's item, so its repo-local components resolve as
they do on publish; without it, the item rules are reported deferred.
Nothing is written. Requires the ``blueprints:read`` permission.

post.description:
Create a new component from scratch in an organization, holding its first draft.

How a component the catalog does not list is authored: one runnable piece
of an app — a service, worker or job — built from a container image
(``spec.workload.source.image``; a bare ``name:tag`` is valid) or a Git
repository the platform builds. The smallest service is a document of
``specVersion: v2``, ``kind: COMPONENT``, ``metadata`` with ``revision: 1``
and a one-sentence ``description``, and ``spec`` with ``type: SERVICE`` and
a ``workload`` naming its ``source.image`` and one ``endpoints`` entry
(``targetPort`` and ``protocol``). Every environment variable the
container reads is an input in ``spec.contract.inputs``, with a
``description``, a ``schema``, an optional ``default`` and
``target.envVar`` naming the variable; a secret input is also
``sensitive: true``. There is no ``workload.envVars``. A workload serving
HTTPS declares its endpoint ``protocol: HTTPS`` with ``tls``: a
``serverName`` the certificate is issued for, or ``verify: NONE`` for a
certificate generated at startup (deploy refuses a verified endpoint with
no ``serverName``). A probe of a login-gated service sends ``auth`` whose
password or token reads a sensitive input. Check a document
first with ``validate_component``; nothing is stored until this call. To
copy a component from the catalog instead, use
``clone_component_from_listing``.

The draft is created at the document's ``metadata.revision``. The ``slug``
must be new to the organization's library; an existing component takes a
new version instead (``create_component_version``). Omit ``slug`` and a
friendly ``adjective-noun`` name is minted, which ``update_component``
can rename while the component has released nothing. A document the schema
accepts is stored even when a semantic rule fails: the returned
``validation`` names what keeps it from publishing. A blueprint can attach
the draft at once (``attach_blueprint_version_component``); publish it
(``publish_component_version``) before that blueprint can publish.

Requires the ``components:create`` permission.

post.description:
Deploy the Blueprint revision a published catalog listing pins.

How an app from the catalog is deployed as it is. Billing starts only
once the Deployment first comes up healthy (ACTIVE), and only the hours
it runs are billed: a refused deploy creates nothing, and a Deployment
that fails before it first runs is never billed. Read the listing's
deploy form first for the ``parameters`` it takes. To change the app
before deploying it, copy it into the library with
``clone_blueprint_from_listing``.

Resolves the deployment — submitted parameters, organization variables,
generated credentials and connections — and on success requests
provisioning in the same transaction, so the returned Deployment is
already in PROVISIONING. A deployment that does not resolve returns 422
with every diagnostic in ``errors`` and the obligations it could not
complete in ``deferred``; nothing is created. A listing whose components
build from git sources is accepted once everything but their images
resolves: the Deployment is returned in DRAFT until they are built and
verified (``status.sources``). If the listing is deprecated, a
``Warning: 299`` header is included per RFC 9111 §5.5.

Open an audited, time-boxed terminal into one running replica.

The body is optional: without one the session is for a browser client with no
stated reason. The response carries the session and a connection, the relay's
URL and a grant good for 60 seconds; offer the grant to the relay as the second
`Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value, after `musher-access.v1`, never in the URL. A
replica holds at most three live sessions, and a session ends after 15 idle
minutes or four hours. Requires `runtimes:exec` and a signed-in user.

post.description: A replica is one running instance of your app's workload, placed on a host. Restart replaces a single replica with a fresh one started from the app's current configuration; nothing else about the app changes. Returns 202 at once: the platform places the replica again, usually on the same host, and the old one stops once it is replaced, so the new replica has a new id. The response is the replica being replaced; its successor appears in `list_replicas` for the same `deploymentId` and `node` once placement binds it. A FAILED or TERMINATED replica cannot be restarted (409). Tenant scope is enforced by the handler — non-members receive 404 to avoid leaking existence.

tags.description:
Make your first authenticated request to the Musher API in five minutes. This guide walks through the minimum viable integration: get a key, send a request, read the response.

## 1. Get an API key

Sign in to the [Musher Console](https://console.musher.dev) and open your organization's **Settings → API Keys**. Click **Create API Key**, name it (e.g. `dev-laptop`), choose the role it acts with, and copy the value — it is only shown once.

Every key is prefixed `mush_` and carries the permissions of the role it is bound to in the issuing organization.

```bash
# Store the key in your shell environment for the rest of this guide.
export MUSHER_API_KEY="mush_..."
```

## 2. Verify the key

The simplest call you can make is `GET /v1/users/me`. It returns the user associated with the key.

```bash
curl -sS https://api.musher.dev/v1/users/me \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MUSHER_API_KEY" \
  | jq
```

A successful response looks like:

```json
{
  "id": "f3a91c8b-8f3d-4d2a-bd91-2c4e1f1f8a91",
  "email": "you@example.com",
  "displayName": "Alex Example",
  "createdAt": "2026-05-13T10:00:00Z"
}
```

If the response is a 401 with `type: "/errors/unauthorized"`, the key is missing, mistyped, or revoked. See the **Authentication** concept for the full auth model.

## 3. Read a list endpoint

List endpoints follow the same shape across the API: cursor-based pagination, camelCase JSON, ISO 8601 timestamps. Fetch the organizations the user belongs to:

```bash
curl -sS "https://api.musher.dev/v1/organizations?limit=5" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MUSHER_API_KEY" \
  | jq
```

```json
{
  "data": [
    {
      "id": "01HV0...",
      "name": "Acme",
      "createdAt": "2026-04-01T12:00:00Z"
    }
  ],
  "meta": {
    "nextCursor": null,
    "hasMore": false
  }
}
```

`meta.nextCursor` is opaque — pass it back as `?cursor=...` to fetch the next page. See the **Pagination** concept for the full contract.

## 4. Explore the reference

Every endpoint here has request and response schemas, real examples, and an in-browser **Try It** console. Sign in (top-right of this page) and Try-It uses your real session — destructive operations are blocked by default while sandbox tenancy is in development.
tags.name: concept-quickstart
tags.x-summary: Make your first authenticated request in five minutes.

tags.description:
The Musher API supports three authentication modes. Pick the one that matches your runtime.

## Bearer token (API key)

The default for server-to-server integrations. Send your key as a `Bearer` token in the `Authorization` header:

```http
Authorization: Bearer mush_8f7a9d3b.kV4uW2pX9Lq...
```

A key is `mush_` followed by an 8-character Base62 public id, a period, and a 43-character Base62 secret. The public id is the part that appears in the Console and in audit records; the secret is shown once, at creation.

Keys are issued in your organization's **Settings → API Keys** in the [Console](https://console.musher.dev): choose **Create API Key**, give it a name, and pick a **role**. The key carries exactly that role's permissions in the organization that issued it — there is no separate key-level scope to configure.

There is no rotate operation. To rotate, create a new key, move your integration to it, then revoke the old one — revocation takes effect on the next request.

## Cookie session

Used automatically by the Musher Console and (when you sign in to this docs site) by the in-browser Try-It console. The session cookie is set by the API at sign-in and is `HttpOnly` + `Secure` + `SameSite=Lax`. You cannot mint these tokens from API code — they come from a successful sign-in flow.

## JWT access token

Issued by a successful sign-in, including sign-in through an OAuth provider. Send the JWT as `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>`. Access tokens live 15 minutes; refresh tokens live 14 days and rotate on every refresh.

## Enumeration protection

Registration always returns `201 Created`, even when the email is already in use. Password recovery always returns `200 OK`, regardless of whether the email matches an account. This prevents attackers from probing the API for valid email addresses.
tags.name: concept-authentication
tags.x-summary: API keys bound to a role, cookie sessions, and JWTs.

tags.description:
All error responses from the Musher API follow [RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457). The content type is `application/problem+json` and the body contains a stable, parseable shape.

## Envelope

```json
{
  "type": "/errors/resource-conflict",
  "title": "Resource Conflict",
  "status": 409,
  "detail": "Email already registered",
  "instance": "/v1/users",
  "traceId": "abc123"
}
```

| Field      | Purpose                                                                     |
| ---------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `type`     | Stable identifier for the error class. Safe to switch on programmatically.   |
| `title`    | Short human-readable summary of the error class.                            |
| `status`   | Mirrors the HTTP status code.                                               |
| `detail`   | Human-readable explanation specific to this occurrence.                     |
| `instance` | The path that produced the error.                                           |
| `traceId`  | Correlation id for the trace in your support ticket.                        |

Some error classes add **extension members** beyond these six — a rate limit carries its retry window, a revision conflict carries both revision numbers. Unknown members are safe to ignore.

## The `type` identifier

`type` is always an absolute-path reference of the form `/errors/{slug}`. It is the primary identifier for the error class, and it is byte-identical in every environment — the same string in local development, staging, and production.

Every slug is documented at `https://docs.musher.dev/reference/errors/{slug}`; the full list lives at [docs.musher.dev/reference/errors](https://docs.musher.dev/reference/errors).

## Best practice

Switch on `type`, not on `detail` — the detail string is human-prose and may change between releases. The `type` identifier is stable and safe to use as a discriminator in retry logic, alerting, and user-facing error mapping.

When a request fails, always log `traceId` alongside your application context. Support tickets are resolved much faster with the trace id attached.
tags.name: concept-errors
tags.x-summary: RFC 9457 ProblemDetail envelope and the type catalog.

tags.description:
Every list endpoint uses **cursor-based** pagination. Cursors are opaque — clients pass them back to the server unchanged. Offset-based pagination is not supported because it produces inconsistent results under concurrent writes.

## Query parameters

| Parameter | Type    | Default | Max | Required |
| --------- | ------- | ------- | --- | -------- |
| `limit`   | integer | 20      | 100 | No       |
| `cursor`  | string  | —       | —   | No       |

`limit` is clamped server-side; a value above 100 returns a 400 with `type: "/errors/invalid-cursor"`.

## Response shape

```json
{
  "data": [
    { "...": "..." }
  ],
  "meta": {
    "nextCursor": "eyJpZCI6Li4u",
    "hasMore": true
  }
}
```

- `data` — array of result objects.
- `meta.nextCursor` — opaque base64-encoded JSON. `null` when no more pages.
- `meta.hasMore` — boolean convenience flag mirroring `nextCursor !== null`.

## Iterating

Treat the cursor as a token. Fetch in a loop until `hasMore` is false:

```bash
cursor=""
while :; do
  response=$(curl -sS "https://api.musher.dev/v1/bundles?limit=50${cursor:+&cursor=$cursor}" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $MUSHER_API_KEY")
  echo "$response" | jq -r '.data[] | .id'
  cursor=$(echo "$response" | jq -r '.meta.nextCursor // empty')
  [ -z "$cursor" ] && break
done
```

## Cursor stability

Cursors bind to the filter set used in the request. If you change a filter mid-iteration (e.g. add `?status=archived`), the server returns an `InvalidCursorError` rather than silently restarting from page 1 — this prevents subtle data-loss bugs in incremental syncs.

If you receive `type: "/errors/invalid-cursor"`, drop the cursor and start over with the new filter set.

## Sort order

Each list endpoint documents its sort key (usually `created_at DESC, id DESC`). Sort order is part of the cursor; clients cannot override it. Endpoints that need a different sort expose a `?sort=` query parameter and document the allowed values in their reference page.
tags.name: concept-pagination

tags.description:
The Musher API does not rate-limit requests today: no request is refused for volume, and responses carry no `RateLimit-*` or `Retry-After` headers. A limit may be introduced later, so write clients that already treat `429 Too Many Requests` correctly rather than assuming it can never happen.

## 429 Too Many Requests

A limited request is answered with `429` and an RFC 9457 Problem Detail of type `/errors/rate-limit-exceeded`. The body carries the standard members only:

```json
{
  "type": "/errors/rate-limit-exceeded",
  "title": "Rate Limit Exceeded",
  "status": 429,
  "detail": "Rate limit exceeded",
  "instance": "/v1/organizations/…/deployments",
  "traceId": "8304680a"
}
```

## Backoff strategy

Retry a `429` with **exponential backoff and full jitter**. Honour a `Retry-After` header if a response ever carries one, and otherwise back off on your own schedule:

```python
import random, time

def with_backoff(call, *, attempts=5, base=0.5, cap=30.0):
    for n in range(attempts):
        response = call()
        if response.status_code != 429:
            return response
        ceiling = float(response.headers.get("Retry-After", base * (2 ** n)))
        time.sleep(min(cap, random.uniform(0, ceiling)))
    raise RuntimeError("max retries exceeded")
```

Do not retry on `4xx` statuses other than 429. They indicate a problem with the request itself, which a delay will not fix. Retry a mutating request with the same `Idempotency-Key`, so that a retry of a request which in fact succeeded replays its response instead of acting twice.
tags.name: concept-rate-limits
tags.x-summary: No request limits today, and how to back off on 429 and 5xx.

tags.description:
Every mutating endpoint (`POST`, `PATCH`, `PUT`, `DELETE`) accepts an `Idempotency-Key` header. Send the same key with the same request body and the server returns the original response — even if the first response was lost in transit.

This is the only safe way to retry writes over an unreliable network.

## How it works

1. Generate a UUID v4 client-side. Do not reuse keys across logically different requests.
2. Send the request with `Idempotency-Key: <uuid>`.
3. If the request succeeds, the response is captured and replayable.
4. If you retry with the same key and same body, the server replays the captured response.
5. Replays surface an `Idempotent-Replayed: true` response header so you know the request was deduplicated.

Only a success is captured. A `4xx` or `5xx` releases the key, so your next attempt runs for real — which means you can correct a rejected request and resubmit it under the same key rather than having to mint a new one.

## Example

```bash
KEY=$(uuidgen)

curl -sS -X POST "https://api.musher.dev/v1/organizations/$ORG_ID/api-keys" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MUSHER_API_KEY" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: $KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "ci-deploy", "roleId": "'"$ROLE_ID"'"}'
```

If the network drops before the response arrives, retry with the same `$KEY` and `$body` and you will get the same `id` back — the server will not create a duplicate key.

## Key lifetime

Idempotency keys are remembered for **24 hours**. Beyond that window the server treats the key as fresh and will re-execute the operation. For long-running retry loops, generate a new key on every logical attempt rather than holding one forever.

## Body mismatch

If you send the same `Idempotency-Key` with a different request body **after that key already succeeded**, the server returns `409 Conflict` with `type: "/errors/idempotency-key-mismatch"`. This usually means a bug in the client — a UUID got reused across two distinct operations. A key whose request was rejected is free again, so correcting a validation error and resubmitting is not a mismatch.

If a request with the same key is still in flight, the server returns `409 Conflict` with `type: "/errors/idempotency-in-progress"` rather than starting a second copy of the same work. Retry after a moment.

## Scope

A key is scoped to the credential that presented it, plus the method and path. Two different callers cannot see each other's cached responses, and the same key sent to two different endpoints is two independent operations.

If your credential changes between the original request and the retry — an expiring session token that refreshed in between — the retry is treated as a fresh request. Retries normally happen within seconds, so this is rare in practice; long-lived `mush_*` API keys are never affected.

## What is not idempotent

- `GET` and `HEAD` are safe by definition; the header is accepted but ignored.
- Responses that stream (`text/event-stream`) or exceed 256 KiB are not captured, so a retry re-executes.
- Webhook delivery from Musher to your endpoints carries its own retry semantics (see the **Webhooks** concept).
tags.name: concept-idempotency
tags.x-summary: Safely retry writes with the Idempotency-Key header.
